extracted.intended_audience: European Commission staff (lead DGs), policy-makers and analysts preparing consultations, impact assessments, evaluations and fitness checks
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for planning, conducting and using stakeholder consultations and evaluations (including fitness checks) in Commission policymaking and impact assessment processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to carry out broad consultations (Article 11 TEU)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Article 11 TEU, the Commission has a duty to carry out broad consultations with interested parties to ensure EU action is coherent and transparent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consulting stakeholders collects evidence, practical experience and data to improve understanding, quality, credibility, acceptance and trust in policy initiatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Call for evidence as entry point
rubrics_metrics.description: The ‘call for evidence’ is the entry point for public consultation and feedback; it combines feedback to call-for-evidence documents and, when required, a public consultation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The call for evidence document is translated into all EU official languages and published on the 'Have Your Say' web portal, which is the single entry point for contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope: what stakeholder consultation covers
rubrics_metrics.description: Stakeholder consultation is a formal process collecting information and views from stakeholders about Commission policies; it explicitly includes environmental and digital aspects where relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Covers public consultations and targeted consultations in preparing policy initiatives or evaluating existing interventions; excludes interinstitutional consultations, certain expert-group opinions, consultations by EU agencies prior to Commission finalisation, and citizens’ initiatives under Article 11(4) TEU.

rubrics_metrics.name: General principles for consultations
rubrics_metrics.description: Relations with stakeholders are governed by four general principles: participation; openness and accountability; effectiveness; coherence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Participation — consult as widely as possible. Openness/accountability — make process and its impact on policymaking transparent, including accessibility for persons with disabilities. Effectiveness — consult when views can still make a difference, considering proportionality and constraints. Coherence — ensure consistency across services in processes, analysis, review and quality control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum standards for consultations
rubrics_metrics.description: Five minimum standards apply to all consultations: clarity, targeting, outreach, sufficient time for participation, publication of contributions and results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarity — documents should be clear and concise; technical questionnaires should include general questions for non-specialists. Targeting — ensure strategy reaches all interested parties. Outreach — awareness-raising and adapted communication channels; publish public consultations on 'Have Your Say'. Sufficient time — as a rule calls for evidence/public consultations are published for 12 weeks. Publication — publish contributions and results on 'Have Your Say' and, if possible, on DG websites.

rubrics_metrics.name: When stakeholder consultation is required
rubrics_metrics.description: Stakeholders should normally be consulted when preparing an initiative accompanied by an impact assessment; for evaluations of broad public interest and fitness checks, public consultation is highly recommended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For very technical or limited-interest initiatives, a targeted consultation may be more suitable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandatory internet-based public consultation (12 weeks) — scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Internet-based public consultation (minimum 12 weeks) is mandatory for initiatives with impact assessments, back-to-back evaluations with impact assessments, consultative communications, and green papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where several consultation steps are required it is not necessary to conduct a 12-week consultation each time; exceptional cases may apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended internet-based public consultation (12 weeks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Internet-based public consultations (minimum 12 weeks) are recommended for evaluations of broad public interest and fitness checks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendation is subject to general rules and exceptional cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feedback durations for specific documents
rubrics_metrics.description: Stakeholders must be able to give feedback on various documents with specified minimum periods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Call for evidence documents for impact assessments, evaluations of broad public interest and fitness checks: 12 weeks (when published with public consultation). Call for evidence for initiatives not accompanied by public consultation: 4 weeks. Draft delegated and implementing acts: 4 weeks (with limited exceptions). Legislative proposals adopted by the College and accompanying final impact assessments: 8 weeks. Feedback on how to improve existing legislation: at any time via 'Have Your Say: Simplify!'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-phase consultation process
rubrics_metrics.description: Consultation process phases: (1) planning the stakeholder consultation and establishing the consultation strategy; (2) conducting the consultation work; (3) informing policymaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each phase consists of steps that provide a framework for high-quality, transparent stakeholder consultation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Key elements of the consultation strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: The consultation strategy key elements must be included in the 'call for evidence' documents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good strategy sets out scope and objectives; identifies all relevant stakeholders; identifies appropriate consultation activities, methods and tools; ensures accessibility; and considers promotion and outreach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Setting consultation scope and objectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine consultation objectives: what is the aim, and which proposal aspects are to be consulted on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objectives could include gathering new ideas, collecting a wide spectrum of views, gathering scientific evidence, data and knowledge, or testing existing ideas and analysis. The type/scope of activities depends on initiative type, timing and context; for initiatives with impact assessments scope must cover elements in Box 5.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandatory scope of consultations for impact assessments
rubrics_metrics.description: For initiatives accompanied by impact assessments, the consultation strategy activities together must cover all elements of the impact assessment process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key issues: the problem to be tackled; subsidiarity and the EU dimension; available policy options and their potential impacts; when modifying existing interventions, scope for efficiency improvements and simplification measures that do not affect achievement of objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandatory scope for fitness checks and evaluations
rubrics_metrics.description: For fitness checks and evaluations of broad public interest the activities must cover the five mandatory evaluation criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mandatory evaluation criteria: relevance, effectiveness, efficiency, coherence, and EU added value. Individual activities may focus on some criteria only, as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stakeholder mapping
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify and map stakeholder groups to determine appropriate consultation methods and tools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult broadly and transparently to seek a whole spectrum of views. Successful mapping involves identifying stakeholder categories relevant to the policy area and prioritising categories to engage with according to interest, expertise or influence, bearing in mind whom it will affect, who will implement it, and who has a stated interest. Research community is an important category to target.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consultation methods: public vs targeted
rubrics_metrics.description: Consultations can be public or targeted; the selected method should reflect objectives and target groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public consultations foster transparency and broad validation but respondents are self-selecting and not representative — assess relevance thoroughly and watch for coordinated campaigns. Targeted consultations allow focused interaction and may tap expertise more efficiently for technical subjects but avoid granting privileged access to some stakeholders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of consultation tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Tools should match the selected method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common tools: consultation documents, questionnaires (written consultations), interviews, meetings, conferences, hearings and other events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeframes for consultations and feedback (Box 6)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specified minimum timeframes for internet-based public consultations and feedback depending on the document and stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Initiatives with impact assessments, evaluations/fitness checks (where relevant), consultative communications and green papers: minimum 12 weeks. Call for evidence documents (impact assessments, evaluations): 12 weeks after publication. Calls for evidence for initiatives not accompanied by public consultation: 4 weeks. Draft delegated acts and implementing acts: 4 weeks. Legislative proposals adopted by College: 8 weeks (after interservice consultation and before Comitology Committee vote).

rubrics_metrics.name: Announcing and communicating consultations
rubrics_metrics.description: Launch should be announced on a dedicated website in a form that accounts for all target audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use communication channels appropriate to reach relevant target groups and adapt formats to audience needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Running consultations and acknowledging contributions
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical organisation requires sufficient resources for replying to questions, solving technical problems and processing contributions (including moderation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allocate sufficient resources for facilitation and technical support; moderation as needed; ensure practical arrangements are in place.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality and testing of consultation documents
rubrics_metrics.description: The quality of consultation documents determines the quality of contributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good practice is to test consultation documents (presentations, surveys, questionnaires) with groups resembling the target audience who were not involved in drafting them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication of contributions
rubrics_metrics.description: Contributions to a consultation must be published, in the language submitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Written contributions should be made public on the dedicated consultation webpage; for consultation events, publish summary minutes and presentations. Respondents should be offered options: publication with personal information or anonymised publication. Data handling must respect data protection rules and be set out in a privacy statement on the consultation page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factual summary report (8-week requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Within 8 weeks of the closure of the public consultation, publish a short factual summary of the key issues raised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This applies to public consultations only; 8-week timeframe is indicative for large numbers of responses. Good practice to publish factual summaries for targeted consultation activities as envisaged in the consultation strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analysing consultation content
rubrics_metrics.description: Input received must be thoroughly analysed and presented objectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise that most consultation responses are not statistically representative; use alternative methods (e.g. Eurobarometer) when representative input is needed. Present results in an objective, unbiased way, briefly describe respondents’ profiles and record all views including dissenting ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Synopsis report and providing feedback to stakeholders
rubrics_metrics.description: Stakeholders should receive adequate and thorough feedback through a synopsis report prepared at the end of consultation activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Synopsis should explain how and to what extent input was taken into account and why suggestions were not taken up. The synopsis report is attached to the impact assessment or evaluation report as an annex and accompanies the Commission’s adoption; otherwise publish as a linked or dedicated SWD. For legislative proposals, the explanatory memorandum should reference the outcome of the stakeholder consultation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose and definition of evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluation is an evidence-based assessment of the extent to which an intervention is effective, efficient, relevant, coherent and has EU added value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluations look at whether EU legislation and programmes are fit for purpose and deliver intended objectives at minimum cost; they consider why changes happened and, if possible, how much changed. Fitness checks are comprehensive evaluations of two or more related interventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate first principle and when evaluation is required
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluation should be conducted before revisions of legislation ('evaluate first'); it is required where demanded by legal basis or by the Financial Regulation for significant spending.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation is required before revisions, where evaluation clauses exist, and for programmes/activities entailing significant spending (indicatively over EUR 5 million).

rubrics_metrics.name: REFIT requirement: look for simplification and burden reduction
rubrics_metrics.description: As part of the REFIT programme, evaluations should specifically look at simplification and burden reduction potential as part of the efficiency analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluations and fitness checks help identify possibilities for simplification and burden reduction without jeopardising benefits; every revision of legislation should in principle be preceded by an evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation procedural steps and governance
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluation work is led by the lead DG(s); evaluations are introduced and validated in Decide and an interservice group should be set up after validation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interservice group should include better regulation support unit, other interested DGs and the Secretariat-General and be involved in key steps including preparing the questionnaire. For evaluations selected for RSB scrutiny, draft report must be submitted to the RSB; interservice consultation cannot be launched before RSB opinion. Publish final evaluation report, call for evidence, related documents and, if applicable, contractor’s final study and RSB opinion centrally (Have Your Say). Feed evaluation results into annual activity reports and identify follow-up actions in annual management plans. Where required by law, transmit a summary report to EP and Council.

rubrics_metrics.name: Key principles for evaluations (quality standards)
rubrics_metrics.description: All evaluations should be of high quality and respect principles: comprehensiveness, proportionality, independence and objectivity, evidence-based approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comprehensiveness — cover at least effectiveness, efficiency, relevance, coherence and EU added value. Proportionality — tailor scope to the intervention, time since implementation and available data; generally wait for ~3 years of data before evaluation. Independence/objectivity — base analysis on all relevant information and conduct without undue influence; report positive and negative elements transparently. Evidence-based — use best available evidence from diverse methods and sources, triangulate, consider biases and uncertainty; use sensitivity/scenario analysis where necessary.
